title: To amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to authorize additional emergency uses for medical products to reduce deaths and severity of injuries caused by agents of war, and for other purposes.
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was introduced. The expanded summary of the House passed version is repeated here.)

(Sec. 1) This bill amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to allow the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to authorize the emergency use of an otherwise unapproved medical product if the Department of Defense (DOD) determines that there is a military emergency involving an agent that may cause imminently life-threatening and specific risk to U.S. forces. If a military emergency is determined to exist, the bill allows DOD to request that the FDA expedite certain procedures for approving medical products that would be reasonably likely to diagnose, prevent, treat, or mitigate such risk. The FDA must take specified actions to facilitate such a request by DOD.

The bill repeals provisions of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018 that allow DOD, rather than the FDA, to authorize the emergency use of an unapproved product under similar circumstances.

Unless DOD determines such meetings to be unnecessary, the FDA shall meet with DOD: (1) semi-annually to conduct a full review of relevant medical products in the DOD portfolio; and (2) quarterly to discuss the development status of regenerative medicine advanced therapy, blood, and vaccine medical products and projects that DOD prioritizes.

summary.headline: This law lets the FDA authorize unapproved medical products for emergency military use when the Department of Defense declares a military emergency involving a dangerous agent of war.
summary.what_it_does: The law amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to let the Food and Drug Administration authorize emergency use of a medical product that is not yet approved, if the Department of Defense determines a military emergency exists involving an agent that could cause life-threatening harm to U.S. forces. The Department of Defense can ask the FDA to speed up its approval steps for products likely to diagnose, prevent, treat, or lessen that risk, and the FDA must take set actions to help. The law also repeals parts of the 2018 National Defense Authorization Act that had let the Department of Defense, instead of the FDA, authorize such emergency uses. It requires the FDA and Department of Defense to meet twice a year to review medical products in the Department's portfolio and every quarter to discuss regenerative medicine, blood, and vaccine products, unless the Department decides those meetings are unnecessary.

who_it_affects.how: They could receive unapproved medical products under FDA emergency authorization when a military emergency involving a dangerous agent of war is declared.
It gains a formal process to request expedited FDA review and emergency authorization of medical products, replacing its earlier authority under the 2018 defense authorization act.
It must take specified steps to help expedite products the Department of Defense requests and must meet with the Department on a set schedule.

who_it_affects.group: Medical product developers and manufacturers working on countermeasures for military threats
who_it_affects.how: Products they develop for these threats may be considered for expedited FDA review and emergency authorization under the new process.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 12, 2017; the summary does not list separate effective dates for specific provisions.
